passage:
The parent-teacher meeting ran late, and Mohit sir was on his fourteenth family when Divyansh's father sat down, Divyansh standing stiffly behind him.
The mid-term report lay open: 41 in science.
'His cousin Saurabh got 92,' the father said, before Mohit sir could speak. 'Same school, same books. Our neighbour's son also. Only this one is like this.'
Divyansh stared at a crack in the classroom floor. His ears had gone red.
Mohit sir answered the father's questions politely. When the father stepped out to take a phone call, the teacher turned to Divyansh and said quietly, 'One result is a result. It isn't you. I've seen your lab work.'
Divyansh looked up, startled.
'Come to the staff room on Monday, after lunch. We'll look at what went wrong in the paper and make a plan for three weeks. Just us.'
Divyansh nodded once.

qa.q: What mark did Divyansh get in science?
qa.a: Divyansh got 41 in science on the mid-term report.

qa.q: What do Divyansh's red ears and staring at the floor suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt ashamed and small while his father compared him with his cousin and the neighbour's son.

qa.q: Why was Mohit sir's quiet word, with a plan for Monday, helpful here?
qa.a: It separated Divyansh from one bad mark and gave him a concrete next step, which comparison could never do.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father see the result differently if he heard what Mohit sir said?
qa.a: He might realise his son has real strengths the teacher has seen, and that comparing him with others only makes the shame worse.

grounding: It shows a teacher watching a teen face family comparison after a bad result and offering a quiet word that one result is not the person, plus a plan.

passage:
Dear Wasim,
I didn't get to talk to you properly at Nani's on Sunday, with everyone there, so I'm writing instead.
I saw your face when Khala started on about Faiz's rank and Ruksar's percentage, and then turned to you and said, 'And yours?' I saw you go quiet and push the rice around your plate. I wanted to say something then and I didn't. I'm sorry.
So here it is now: one bad board result is one result. It isn't the whole of you. You're the one who fixed Nana's radio and taught me how to use a spreadsheet. That's still true after a 58 in maths.
If you want, come over on Saturday afternoon. We'll look at what went wrong, together, and plan what you want to do about the supplementary exam. No lectures, promise.
Your Devika didi

qa.q: What did Wasim do at the table when Khala asked about the result?
qa.a: Wasim went quiet and pushed the rice around the plate.

qa.q: Why does Devika say sorry in her letter?
qa.a: She feels guilty that she wanted to speak up at Nani's on Sunday and didn't, while Wasim was being compared.

qa.q: What does Devika offer Wasim as a next step?
qa.a: She invites Wasim on Saturday afternoon to look at what went wrong together and plan for the supplementary exam, with no lectures.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel reading this letter after the lunch at Nani's?
qa.a: Wasim may feel less alone and less judged, knowing at least one person in the family sees Wasim as more than a maths mark.

grounding: It shows an older didi who saw a teen being compared with others after a bad result, offering a quiet word that the result is not the person and help to plan.

passage:
The holidays? Honestly, one afternoon stuck with me. My cousin Bhavna had just got her Class 10 results, and they weren't good. Sixty-two per cent. At Dadi's house that Sunday every aunty had a comparison ready. "Pinky got ninety-four." "Our neighbour's son has already joined engineering coaching." Bhavna kept passing the samosas and smiling like a shop mannequin.
I'm Varun, I'm twenty-three, and I remember that smile from my own bad year. So after lunch I found her on the back steps, just sitting. I didn't give advice. I said, "One result is one result. It isn't you." She didn't answer, but her shoulders came down a little.
Then I asked if she wanted to sit with me on Tuesday and look at which subjects she actually liked, and plan from there. She said, "Maybe." On Tuesday she came.

qa.q: What percentage did Bhavna get in her Class 10 results?
qa.a: Sixty-two per cent.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling while watching Bhavna smile through the comparisons?
qa.a: Varun felt a painful recognition and concern, remembering a similar bad year and sensing that her smile was hiding hurt.

qa.q: What turning point does Varun offer at this stage?
qa.a: A quiet word that one result isn't Bhavna, followed by an offer to sit on Tuesday and plan from the subjects she likes.

qa.q: What is the lunch like for Bhavna?
qa.a: Painful and humiliating; she has to keep smiling and serving while relatives compare her marks with other children's.

grounding: A cousin watches a teen face relatives' comparisons after a bad result, then offers a quiet word that one result is not her and a plan.

passage:
I teach Hemant's class, so I was at the table when his mother, Chandrika, came for the report card. He had failed two subjects in the pre-boards. She didn't raise her voice. She just said, "His sister topped this same school. I don't know where we went wrong with him." Hemant sat with his hands between his knees, staring at the floor tiles. I couldn't tell if he was angry or just tired.
When she stepped out to take a call, I leaned over and said quietly, "One pre-board is not who you are, Hemant. It only tells us what to fix."
He glanced up, surprised.
I told him I stay back on Thursdays, and we could make a plan for the two subjects, week by week. He didn't say yes. But on Thursday at four he was waiting outside the staffroom with his notebook.

qa.q: How many subjects did Hemant fail in the pre-boards?
qa.a: Two subjects.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling while Chandrika compared Hemant with his sister?
qa.a: The narrator felt uneasy and concerned, unsure whether Hemant was angry or tired, but sure he needed a kinder word.

qa.q: What made the narrator's quiet word useful at this stage?
qa.a: It separated Hemant from the result and came with a concrete offer to plan the two subjects on Thursdays.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant to sit through his mother's comparison?
qa.a: Humiliating and heavy; he stares at the floor while being measured against his sister in front of a teacher.

grounding: A teacher watches a teen hear his mother compare him with his sister after a bad result, and offers a quiet word and a plan.

passage:
Monday. Francis, who teaches maths at the school in Panaji, saw Dhruv come back after the term results with his collar up and earphones in, though they weren't allowed. He had dropped from ninety to fifty-one. Francis let the earphones pass.
Wednesday. At the parent meeting, Dhruv's father said, loud enough for the corridor, "His cousin in Mumbai scores ninety-eight and this one is busy with football." Dhruv gave a short, hard laugh and walked out to the water cooler. Francis watched him drink three cups he didn't want.
Friday. After class, Francis stopped by Dhruv's desk. "One bad term is one bad term. It isn't who you are." Dhruv shrugged. "I'm free Saturday mornings. Want to look at the paper and plan next term? After football practice, if you like."
Dhruv looked up. "Saturday after ten?"

qa.q: What did Dhruv's marks drop from and to?
qa.a: From ninety to fifty-one.

qa.q: What was Francis thinking while watching Dhruv drink three cups at the cooler?
qa.a: Francis felt concerned, sensing that Dhruv's hard laugh was covering hurt and embarrassment after the comparison.

qa.q: What turning point does Francis offer on Friday?
qa.a: A quiet word that one bad term isn't who Dhruv is, plus a Saturday offer to look at the paper and plan, fitted around football.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv at the parent meeting?
qa.a: He feels exposed and humiliated as his father compares him with a cousin where others can hear.

grounding: Over a week a teacher watches a teen face his father's comparison after a bad result, then gives a quiet word and an offer to plan.

passage: "Harsha, you asked how I became the cousin everyone calls when results come out. It started one Diwali, when I was twenty and my cousin Keshav was sixteen. His board results had come out badly that week. At the family lunch, Mausi, Mama, everybody went round the table: 'Sharma ji's son got ninety-five.' 'Your sister topped at your age.' Keshav kept his eyes on his plate and didn't eat. I felt sick watching it. After lunch I found him alone on the roof. I didn't give advice. I said, 'One result is not you, Keshav. I know you.' Then: 'Want to sit down next week and plan what's next? Only if you want.' He nodded. We made a plan with his teacher. Your Madhav chacha has kept that habit ever since."

qa.q: What did a relative say about Sharma ji's son?
qa.a: That Sharma ji's son got ninety-five.

qa.q: What did young Madhav feel watching the lunch-table comparisons?
qa.a: He felt sick and upset, watching Keshav stare at his plate while the relatives compared.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made a difference for Keshav?
qa.a: Madhav found him alone, said one result was not him and offered to plan next steps together, which led to a plan with his teacher.

qa.q: What was the lunch like for Keshav?
qa.a: Keshav felt humiliated and small, keeping his eyes on his plate and unable to eat.

grounding: Shows a cousin watching a teen compared with others after a bad result, then offering a quiet word and help planning next steps.
